ai.definition: Nanotechnology in medicine involves the application of nanoscale materials to improve the efficacy and safety of medical treatments, particularly in drug delivery and diagnostic tools.
ai.howItWorks: Nanoparticles are engineered with specific properties that allow them to target diseased cells or tissues precisely. In drug delivery, they can encapsulate drugs and release them slowly over time. For diagnostics, nanoparticles can be used as contrast agents for imaging techniques like MRI or as sensors in point-of-care tests.
ai.problemSolved: Nanotechnology addresses the limitations of traditional medical treatments by providing more targeted therapies that reduce side effects and improve patient outcomes.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves synthesizing nanoparticles with controlled size, shape, and surface chemistry. Techniques include bottom-up approaches like self-assembly and top-down methods such as lithography or milling.
ai.buildProcess: The build process typically includes synthesis of the nanoparticle core, functionalization to attach targeting ligands or imaging agents, and quality control testing for size distribution, stability, and biocompatibility.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include raw material costs, advanced equipment for synthesis, specialized lab facilities, and regulatory compliance. Customization for specific applications also adds complexity and cost.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive with increasing clinical adoption and expanding research areas, but challenges remain in standardizing manufacturing processes and ensuring safety.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are evolving, with agencies like the FDA requiring rigorous testing for biocompatibility, efficacy, and safety of nanomedicines.
ai.risks: Risks include potential toxicity from nanoparticles, variability in manufacturing processes, and the need for long-term studies to assess their impact on human health.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable; successful products can be highly profitable due to high margins but require significant upfront investment. Market penetration depends on clinical validation and reimbursement rates.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on improving biocompatibility, enhancing targeting capabilities, and integrating nanotechnology with other advanced medical technologies like AI for personalized medicine.

glossary.def: A particle with at least one dimension in the nanometer scale (1-100 nm).
The process of administering a drug to achieve a therapeutic effect.
The ability of a material or device to perform with an appropriate host response in a specific application without eliciting harmful effects.

subsystems.name: Nanoparticle carrier
subsystems.role: encapsulates or carries the active agent and determines where it goes in the body.

subsystems.name: Payload
subsystems.role: the drug, gene or imaging agent that does the work.

subsystems.name: Surface functionalization
subsystems.role: keeps the particle stable in blood and helps it find the right cells.

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and formulation
subsystems.role: produces uniform particles at the right size and with the right dose.

subsystems.name: Characterization and quality control
subsystems.role: checks size, charge and drug loading before use.

subsystems.name: Delivery and release
subsystems.role: gets the particle to the target and releases its payload.

buildSteps.title: Select platform and payload
buildSteps.detail: Choose lipid, polymer or inorganic nanoparticles based on the drug or imaging agent and the target tissue.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the nanoparticle
buildSteps.detail: For lipid nanoparticles, mix lipids in ethanol with nucleic acid in aqueous buffer using a microfluidic device; for polymer nanoparticles, use emulsification or nanoprecipitation.

buildSteps.title: Load the payload
buildSteps.detail: Incorporate the drug, mRNA or contrast agent during assembly or adsorb it onto the particle afterwards.

buildSteps.title: Coat and target
buildSteps.detail: Attach PEG chains and targeting molecules such as antibodies or peptides to the surface.

buildSteps.title: Purify
buildSteps.detail: Remove unencapsulated drug and solvents by dialysis or tangential flow filtration.

buildSteps.title: Characterize
buildSteps.detail: Measure size (typically 50–200 nm), surface charge and encapsulation efficiency.

buildSteps.title: Sterilize and package
buildSteps.detail: Filter-sterilize and, if needed, lyophilize for storage.

buildSteps.title: Scale up
buildSteps.detail: Transition from bench to clinical manufacturing under good manufacturing practice (GMP).

prerequisites.why: lipid and polymer nanoparticles are made routinely for approved products.
many materials are safe, but long-term clearance and toxicity are not fully understood for all.
antibodies and peptides exist, but attaching them without losing function or triggering an immune response is hard.
crossing the blood-brain barrier or reaching solid tumours efficiently remains a major challenge.
microfluidic and GMP production exist, but reproducibility and scale-up for complex particles are difficult.
regulators have frameworks for some nanomedicines, but characterizing and approving complex particles is still evolving.

pathway.milestone: approved nanoparticle drug delivery (liposomal chemotherapy, mRNA lipid nanoparticles) and iron oxide contrast agents
pathway.unlocks: targeted delivery and improved safety for some cancers and vaccines.

pathway.milestone: targeted nanoparticles for cancer and genetic diseases reach late-stage trials and approval
pathway.unlocks: therapy that acts only on diseased cells, reducing side effects.

pathway.milestone: nanoparticles that cross the blood-brain barrier
pathway.unlocks: treatments for brain tumours and neurodegenerative diseases.

pathway.milestone: theranostic nanoparticles that diagnose and treat at the same time, and personalized nanomedicine
